name: Milan
info: Milan is a city in the north-western Po Valley of northern Italy, settled by a Celtic tribe around 590 BCE, a Roman imperial seat, the capital of a Renaissance duchy and now the capital of Lombardy.

facts.founded: Around 590 BCE a Celtic tribe of the Insubres group, of the Golasecca culture, settled it as Medhelanon; in the legend reported by Livy it was founded by Bellovesus in the reign of Tarquinius Priscus.
facts.where: In the north-western part of the Po Valley in Lombardy, northern Italy, about halfway between the river Po and the foothills of the Alps, between the Ticino to the west and the Adda to the east.
facts.known: Mediolanum as an imperial seat; the Edict of Milan of 313; Bishop Ambrose; the Visconti and Sforza dukes; Leonardo da Vinci’s Last Supper; the Cathedral and the Castello Sforzesco; the Five Days of 1848
facts.today: Milan is the capital of Lombardy and the second-largest city of Italy, with about 1.36 million people in the city proper.

t: The Celtic settlement of Medhelanon was taken by the Romans in 222 BCE; as Mediolanum it became an imperial seat under Maximian, and the Edict of Milan was issued from it in 313.

After the destruction of 1162 and a long struggle between the della Torre and the Visconti, the Visconti became dukes in 1395 and the Sforza took the city in 1450, before Spanish, Austrian and French rule.
The Five Days of 1848 and the defeat of the Austrians in 1859 brought Milan into the Kingdom of Italy, and in the 19th and 20th centuries it became the country’s industrial and financial centre.
dyk: Under the cathedral lie the ruins of the ancient church of Saint Tecla and the baptistery where Augustine of Hippo was baptised.
ev: A Celtic tribe of the Insubres settles Medhelanon
The Romans under the consul Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus capture the settlement
Constantine issues the Edict of Milan from Mediolanum
Frederick I Barbarossa brings the destruction of much of the city
Francesco Sforza conquers Milan and ends the Ambrosian Republic

The Five Days rebellion forces Radetzky to withdraw temporarily
After the Battle of Solferino Milan and the rest of Lombardy are incorporated into Piedmont-Sardinia

sections.origins:
Milan stands in the north-western part of the Po Valley, about halfway between the river Po to the south and the foothills of the Alps and the great lakes to the north, with the Ticino to the west and the Adda to the east. The land is flat and its highest point is 122 m above sea level. Five watercourses lay near the site: the Seveso and the Lambro to the east, and the Pudiga, the Nirone and the Olona to the west. Three hypotheses are offered for the choice of place: a line of springs on a spit of land that overlooked a swamp, the five watercourses, or an existing Celtic sanctuary near the modern Piazza della Scala.

Around 590 BCE a Celtic tribe of the Insubres group, belonging to the Golasecca culture, settled the place as Medhelanon. In the legend reported by Livy, the Gaulish king Ambicatus sent his nephew Bellovesus into northern Italy, and Bellovesus allegedly founded the settlement in the reign of Tarquinius Priscus. The settlement grew around a sanctuary, a wooded ellipse with a central clearing and axes of 443 m and 323 m, aligned on the heliacal risings of Antares and Capella. About two centuries later houses were built around it, a temple of the goddess Belisama and a fortified building with a moat. Excavation under the Roman forum found wooden houses of the 5th century BCE, and near the Royal Palace the remains of houses and a furnace of the 5th and 4th centuries BCE.
sections.growth:
The Roman Mediolanum became the most important centre of Cisalpine Gaul and a hub in the road network of northern Italy, and in 49 BCE it became a municipium. In the Augustan age it was famous for its schools and had a theatre and an amphitheatre of 129.5 by 109.3 m, the third largest in Roman Italy. Maximian, left at Milan by Diocletian, enlarged the city to 375 acres inside a new stone wall of about 4.5 km, and built a circus of 470 by 85 m, the Baths of Hercules and a large complex of imperial palaces. In the time of Ambrose and Theodosius I the city reached the height of its ancient power.

From the 12th century until the 16th Milan was one of the largest European cities. A period of peace followed the destruction of 1162, and the city prospered as a centre of trade because of its position; its chief industries were armaments and wool. Under the Sforza mulberry growing and silk processing developed, the Sforza Castle and the Ospedale Maggiore were completed, and Leonardo da Vinci worked in the city from 1482 until 1499.

After unification a railway network made Milan the rail hub of northern Italy, and with the Gotthard tunnel of 1882 and the Simplon tunnel of 1906 a major rail hub of southern Europe. The first power station in continental Europe opened there in 1883. The population rose from 1.3 million in 1951 to 1.7 million in 1967 and peaked at 1,743,427 in 1973.
sections.rulers:
The Romans took the settlement in 222 BCE. In 286 Diocletian moved the capital of the Western Roman Empire from Rome to Mediolanum, leaving his colleague Maximian there, and in 402 Honorius moved the imperial residence to Ravenna. The Ostrogoths held the city until 539, and the Lombards conquered it in the summer of 569; they made Ticinum their capital in 572 and left Milan to the governance of its archbishops. It surrendered to Charlemagne and the Franks in 774.

The commune emerged in the 11th century and was confirmed after the Peace of Constance in 1183. In 1259 Martino della Torre was elected Capitano del Popolo and ruled with autocratic powers. Ottone Visconti, made archbishop in 1262, won the city for his family at the Battle of Desio in 1277. In 1395 Gian Galeazzo Visconti became the first Duke of Milan. After the death of Filippo Maria Visconti in 1447 the Ambrosian Republic followed, until Francesco Sforza conquered the city in 1450.

The Italian Wars brought French rule from 1500 until the Battle of Pavia in 1525, and the Sforza line ended in 1535. The city then passed to the Spanish Habsburgs, and in 1713 and 1714 the Treaties of Utrecht and Rastatt confirmed Austrian sovereignty. Milan was the capital of the Napoleonic Cisalpine Republic and Kingdom of Italy from 1797, and of Lombardy-Venetia under Austria from 1815. It joined Piedmont-Sardinia in 1859 and the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.
sections.life:
Christian communities existed in Mediolanum in Roman times, and the first bishop with a firm historical presence is Merocles, at the Council of Rome of 313. In the mid-4th century the Arian controversy divided them, and at times there were rival bishops. Ambrose, bishop from 374 to 397, quelled the Arians and reshaped the centre, building the basilicas at the city gates: Sant’Ambrogio, San Nazaro in Brolo, San Simpliciano and Sant’Eustorgio. About five million Catholics still use the Ambrosian Rite, which differs slightly from the Roman Rite.

Water was abundant, so Mediolanum needed no aqueducts: springs and nearby rivers and streams supplied it, and the Romans led the Seveso, the Nirone and the Olona towards the moat of the walls. The Navigli, a system of navigable canals, gave the city centre its concentric layout; most are now covered. The street plan still followed the Celtic sanctuary in some places up to the 19th century.

In the late 18th and 19th centuries Milan was a centre of intellectual and literary life. Cesare Beccaria wrote Dei delitti e delle pene, Pietro Verri published the periodical Il Caffè, and Alessandro Manzoni wrote The Betrothed in the 1820s. Carlo Porta wrote poems in the Lombard language. Under Maria Theresa the Teatro alla Scala, the Brera Academy and the Braidense Library were founded or sponsored. From the 1950s over 400,000 people came from rural southern Italy.
sections.crises:
In 402 the Visigoths besieged Milan, and in 452 Attila besieged it. The Gothic War brought the greatest break with the imperial past: in 539 the Ostrogoths conquered and destroyed the city. In 1162 Frederick I Barbarossa brought the destruction of much of Milan. The Milanese had destroyed Lodi, fought Pavia, Cremona and Como, and captured Empress Beatrice and forced her to ride a donkey backwards through the city. A fire then destroyed the storehouses that held the entire food supply, and within a few days Milan had to surrender.

Faction followed. In 1252 heretics assassinated the Inquisitor later known as Saint Peter Martyr, and in 1256 the archbishop and leading nobles were expelled. The conflict between the della Torre and the Visconti became a civil war lasting more than a decade. The Great Plague of 1629 to 1631 killed an estimated 60,000 people out of a population of 130,000 and is considered one of the last outbreaks of the plague pandemic that began with the Black Death.

In May 1898 a riot over the rising cost of living ended in the Bava Beccaris massacre, in which at least 80 demonstrators and two soldiers were killed and 450 wounded, according to government sources. In the Second World War Allied bombing caused extensive damage, and German forces occupied the city after Italy’s surrender in 1943. On 12 December 1969 a bomb at the National Agrarian Bank in Piazza Fontana killed 17 people and injured 88.
sections.legacy:
From Mediolanum Constantine issued the Edict of Milan in 313, which granted tolerance to all religions in the Empire. Ambrose left the Ambrosian Rite and the churches at the city’s gates. The cathedral, built from 1386 to 1877, is the largest church in Italy and the most important example of Gothic architecture in the country. The Castello Sforzesco grew from a Visconti fortress, and Leonardo painted The Last Supper for the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie. Napoleon crowned himself King of Italy in the cathedral on 26 May 1805.

The Teatro alla Scala, inaugurated in 1778, became a centre of opera with premieres of Bellini, Donizetti, Rossini and Verdi. The Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II was built between 1865 and 1877, and the Arco della Pace was completed in 1838. Corriere della Sera was first published in 1876. After 1945 the city was rebuilt quickly and La Scala reopened in 1946.

Milan is the capital of Lombardy and the seat of the Metropolitan City of Milan. It has about 1.36 million people in the city proper and is the second-largest city of Italy. Little of the Roman city survives above ground, among it the Colonne di San Lorenzo.

summary: Milan, in the north-western Po Valley, began as the Celtic Medhelanon and became the Roman Mediolanum, an imperial seat under Maximian. Ruled by the Visconti and Sforza dukes and then by Spain, Austria and France, it joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1861 and became its industrial and financial centre.
references: Evelyn S Welch, Art and authority in Renaissance Milan (Yale University Press, New Haven, Connecticut, 1995)
notes: START: the history article says Medhelanon was settled about 590 BC, and also (after Livy) founded about 600 BC by Belloveso; the city article ties Bellovesus to the reign of Tarquinius Priscus (616 to 579 BC). I used c. 590 BCE and kept the legend unattributed to a year.
Capital of the Western Roman Empire: the city article's lead says AD 284 to 402; its body and the history article say 286 (Diocletian). I used 286.

539 sack: the history article says Uraias carried out attacks with losses of about 300,000 men according to Procopius; the city article says after capitulation 300,000 male citizens were executed and the women sold. The articles disagree, so I left the figure out and wrote only that the Ostrogoths conquered and destroyed the city.
452: the history article says Attila besieged the city; the city article says he sacked and devastated it. I wrote only besieged.

Return to Austria: the history article says 1814 (Congress of Vienna) and also that the constitution of the Austrian States in Italy was announced on 7 April 1815; the city article says 1815. I wrote Lombardy-Venetia from 1815 and avoided a return date.

The Napoleonic capital dates (1796 Transpadane Republic, 1797 to 1802 Cisalpine Republic) come from the history article; the city article says Cisalpine Republic from 1796. I wrote 1797 for the Cisalpine Republic.

Louis XII is never named in the articles, only Louis of Orléans and later King Francis I; the 1500 claim and 1525 end of French rule are as the articles give them. The history article says the duchy then returned to Francesco II Sforza, who died ten years later; the city article says the Sforza line went extinct in 1535. Compatible.

dyk: Augustine's baptism is stated only in passing as ruins in the crypt of the Duomo of the baptistery 'where St. Augustine of Hippo was baptized'; I attributed it to the account of the city's churches.

Verdi, the Bava Beccaris figures ('according to government sources'), the plague figures ('estimated') and the 1,743,427 peak in 1973 are as the articles give them. The 1.36 million present population is rounded from 1,362,863 in the city article, written without the year.

Left out: tourism, sport, fashion and economy rankings, airports, the present government, climate and the long lists of museums, companies and districts. The Expo of 1906 and 2015 and the 2026 Olympics were left out as events of little weight for the city's history.
